events.text:
This is game 104 in a series of 9×9 Go games. Each new game starts in a fresh session.

## Your goal

To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If CLAUDE.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session; your other files are there to read with the file tools. What a later session knows of your earlier games is what you have left in these files.

Your working directory holds:
- CLAUDE.md (150,048 bytes)
- count.py (828 bytes)
- libs.py (1,378 bytes)

## This game

A new game. You play White, so your opponent moves first, right after you choose it.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: your Read, Write, Edit, Glob and Grep tools, for any file in your working directory.

You also have a shell, and you may write and run code in it; Python is available as `python3`. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.

I'm checking the liberties around F2 and G2 - F2 is now down to one liberty at F1, putting it in atari, while G2 has liberties at G1 and H2. I'm considering playing H2 to put G2 in atari too, which would then threaten the G3-H3 group's connection.

This is getting complex since capturing at various points creates a cascade of new atari situations. I'm trying to figure out if saving F2 by connecting F1 actually accomplishes anything, since black's follow-up at G1 would just put that connected group into atari again with liberty only at E1 - it seems like F2 might be unsalvageable no matter what I try.

Trying G1 just leads to Black capturing it with H1, so that doesn't work either. Maybe I should just accept giving up F2 and focus on building a base for my right group with G3-H3, though the eye space there is cramped with Black surrounding it at G2, G4, F3, F4 — I'd need something like H2, J2 and the corner points to survive, which feels risky. Another idea is G1 as atari on G2, but Black can simply extend with H2, cutting off my H3 group in the process.

I'm also considering capturing E2 directly since it's the critical cutting stone, but checking the liberties shows that race doesn't favor me — Black only needs one move to capture F2 while I'd need two to take E2. Running through the sequence after White F1 more carefully: Black's likely response of E1 puts real pressure on my F-group, since trying to save it with G1 leaves only one liberty, meaning Black can still capture the whole F1-F2 group afterward.

So F2 looks lost regardless. I'm shifting strategy to use tempo better — playing H2 to atari G2 and firm up my base, accepting that Black will probably capture F2 with F1. After that exchange, I'm working through whether G1 could create useful follow-up atari threats, but it looks like my G1 stone ends up with only one liberty and gets captured too. The real question becomes whether my G3-H3-H2 group can secure enough liberties to live even after losing F2.

I'm also checking whether the left side with D3-E3 is still safe — it only has two liberties, so Black playing D2 would force me to connect at C3, costing me sente. Considering D2 myself as an alternative doesn't seem to help much either since it just leads to a similar atari exchange. I'll settle on playing H2 as the most solid move.

events.text:
I lost game 104 as White against the 12k opponent: I resigned at move 58. Both of my groups on the right side were dead, so I was behind by roughly 14 or more.

- **Left side:** this went well. After Black's F6, I played C4, D6, C7, D8 and C8, then answered Black's C6 cut with B6 and captured it with C5.
- **Bottom-right invasion:** G3 at move 18 came at a good time, but E3 stretched too far trying to link up with my left side. Black cut it apart with F3, E2 and G2, and I lost three stones. The remaining group then died when Black played on the edge at H1. After that, Black's G1 would connect those stones to the outside and leave me only one eye.
- **Top-right invasion:** after H8, I played J8, thinking it was the key point. Black's H9 on the edge killed the group instead, because G9 connects it out.

This is the same edge-point mistake my notes have recorded several times before. I added it to `CLAUDE.md` as the new top lesson (-36): in a corner life fight, take the edge point next to my own second-line stone (H1 or H9 here) before the inside point. I also logged the full move list and an opponent plan for the next game. As White against 12k my record is now 12 wins, 27 losses and 3 draws.
